To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the scaffoldins of the mesophilic anaerobe A. cellulolycticus include a novel type of adaptor protein that connects the enzyme-recognizing scaffoldin to an anchoring scaffoldin, which is anchored to the cell surface by a S-layer homology module.

the scaffoldin genes of A. cellululyticus encode three different scaffoldin proteins and that the cellulosome system includes an unusual type of adaptor protein that links the primary scaffoldin to the anchoring scaffoldin.
a new type of adaptor protein was identified in the cellulosome system, and the presence of the coesins and the consured S-layer homology module implies that the protein acts as an anchorage protein.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms that underlie cellulose degradation in anaerobic bacteria.
the elucidation of the molecular organization of the cellulosome system in the mesophillic cellulolytic anaereobes, Acetivibro cellulolyticus, and Clostridium acetobutylicum.
the molecular biology of the cellulosome, a supramolecular complex that is involved in the degradation of plant cell wall polysaccharides.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the cellulosome system is a highly flexible and dynamic supramolecular structure, which has been evolved by a multitude of bacteria to cope with the challenge of degrading the most abundant polymer in nature, cellulose.
the supramolecular organization of the cellulosome is a flexible and dynamic process that is adapted to the specific requirements of the particular cellulolytic bacterium.
the cellulose degrading systems in the various cellulolytic bacteria are not identical, and the cellulosomes are not a unique, uniform, and invariant supramolecular structure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cellulase systems in different cellulolytic bacteria are highly variable in their supramolecular organization, but all are based on the cohesin-dockerin module as the key structural element.
the A. celluloliticus cellulosome is the largest and most complex cellulosome system described to date.
the A. cellululoticus cellulosome represents the most complex system known so far.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cellulosome is a highly flexible supramolecular structure.
a single type of scaffoldin can act as a primary scaffoldin, a secondary scaffoldin, or a cell surface-anchoring scaffoldin, depending on the bacterial cellulolytic species.
the cellulosome system is not limited to the organization of a single scaffoldin and that a number of variations in the architecture are possible.
